national.title: Zelensky urges US and Musk to lift Starlink restrictions and be on 'right side of history'
national.summary: The Ukrainian president says the slowed-down internet is making it difficult to stop Russian attacks.
national.body:
A crucial US satellite internet service is still operating too slowly and affecting Ukraine's ability to stop Russian attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

"We are counting on these restrictions being lifted. The protection of lives and Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this," he said.

The issue over the speed of the Starshield system - a military-grade service developed by Elon Musk's Starlink and provided to Ukraine by the US government - has been rumbling on for weeks.

"It is important to be on the right side of history," Zelensky said.

The White House and the administration have nothing to do with the reported slowdown, the BBC understands.

US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says

Published 1 day ago US President Donald Trump on Monday said he did not know of any restrictions, saying: "I haven't heard that."

Ukraine uses the normal Starlink service for communications on the battlefield, while Starshield is used for the interception of drones in Ukraine airspace.

national.title: High court rejects challenge to Maryland gun ban in sensitive places
national.summary: The Supreme Court left in place a lower court decision that upheld the measure banning guns in sensitive places.
national.body: Washington — The Supreme Court on Monday turned away a challenge to Maryland laws that prohibit firearms in sensitive places like schools, parks and government buildings.In rejecting the appeal from a group of Maryland residents and gun rights groups, the high court leaves in place a lower court decision that upheld the rules. Justice Clarence Thomas said that while he agrees with the Supreme Court's decision not to hear the case, he is "skeptical" of the constitutionality of sensitive-place restrictions and urged the court to consider the scope of states' authority to ban firearms in those locations in a more "narrowly focused case.""I harbor serious doubts that our Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation supports many of these sweeping restrictions," he wrote in a statement. "In an appropriate case, this Court should consider whether particular sensitive-place laws are consistent with the right to public carry."The Supreme Court last year struck down a Hawaii law that required concealed-carry permit holders to receive permission before bringing their firearms onto private property open to the public.At issue in the case was a set of Maryland laws that limit the places where guns can be carried in public. The state prohibits firearms from being brought on school property, at public demonstrations and on public transit, as well as in parks, museums and casinos.Another set of limits was enacted in 2023, in the wake of the Supreme Court's landmark 2022 decision that recognized for the first time that the Second Amendment protects the right to carry a gun outside the home. Under the new restrictions, people are prohibited from carrying firearms at daycare and medical facilities, government buildings or other places where the public gathers for "entertainment, educational enrichment or other collective social pursuits."On the same day Maryland's latest restrictions were signed into law, two sets of plaintiffs filed lawsuits arguing they violated the Second Amendment. The suits targeted 10 categories of places.The two cases were consolidated, and a federal district court declined to block the limits on museums, healthcare facilities, public transit, state parks, entertainment venues, school grounds and government buildings. national.title: Forensic expert says his analysis raises doubts about how Epstein died
national.summary: Professor Michael Freeman tells BBC Newsnight that he believes the convicted sex offender's injuries are consistent with a homicide.
national.body:
This article contains distressing details and references to suicide

A forensic expert has said he believes that convicted sex offender Jeffery Epstein's death in prison was the result of a homicide, not suicide.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, Professor Michael Freeman said that after reviewing the New York City medical examiner's file he believes Epstein was strangled, most likely from behind.

The medical examiner who carried out the autopsy concluded in 2019 that Epstein's injuries were consistent with suicide and there was no evidence of the defensive wounds expected if his death had been a homicide.

Epstein was found dead in prison on 10 August 2019 in New York as he awaited trial on sex trafficking charges.

Dr Barbara Sampson, chief medical examiner at the time of Epstein's autopsy, who ruled that Epstein's death was a suicide, has previously said: "I stand firmly behind our determination of the cause and manner of death for Mr. Epstein." The BBC has approached Sampson for further comment.

Freeman has served as a cause-of-death expert to attorneys-general in the US for death in police custody cases, including George Floyd in Minnesota.

He published his research and the New York City medical examiner's files after presenting his findings at University College London on Monday evening.

national.title: Lindsay Clancy to face retrial next year for deaths of her three children
national.summary: The 36-year-old's first trial this year fell apart when a 12-person jury failed to reach a verdict.
national.body:
Warning: This story contains details some readers may find distressing.

Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman accused of murdering her three children, will face a retrial next year, a judge has said, after a jury deadlocked last time in a case that gripped the nation.

The judge set a trial date for 29 March 2027, though the district attorney did not explicitly say what charges Clancy would face.

Prosecutors said they wanted a jury trial, and the defence said they took that to mean Clancy, 36, would again face first-degree murder charges.

Five-year-old Cora, Dawson, three, and eight-month-old Callan were strangled at the family home on 24 January 2023. The defence argues she had severe postpartum psychosis.

"I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury, that it's an indirect comment from the DA [district attorney] that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments, so we will pick a trial date," defence lawyer Kevin Reddington said at Monday's hearing.

Prosecutors wanted a May trial date, but Judge William Sullivan decided on March instead. The judge is due to retire in June.

Clancy was charged in the first trial with three counts of first-degree-murder, which is the intentional and premeditated killing of another person.

national.title: Trump backs return of ex-Nvidia boss after 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign launched
national.summary: A number of tech figures want the board of the AI chip giant to give Jensen Huang his job back.
national.body:
US President Donald Trump has said he "would certainly not mind" seeing Jensen Huang handed back his job as allies of the former Nvidia chief executive called for him to be reinstated.

Huang resigned as boss of the AI chip giant last week after the emergence of two affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of spying for China and another allegedly with one of his employees.

It created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms, which is a key part of the AI rollout, but the BBC has been told Nvidia's board is not considering reinstating Huang.

Meanwhile the Trump administration on Monday said it will further restrict China's ​access to AI chips from companies like Nvidia.

Fellow tech bosses, including SpaceX's Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have backed a campaign to get Nvidia's board to "Bring Jensen Back".

The pair were among more than 175,000 signatories of an open letter calling for the board to reinstate Huang while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.

President Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back.

"I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that," he told reporters as he left the White House.

national.title: Freeman Johnson, the oldest of the dwindling number of Pearl Harbor survivors, dies at 106
national.summary: Freeman Johnson was below deck working on a boiler of the USS St. Louis when the Japanese attack happened in December 1941.
national.body:
Michael Casey, Associated Press Michael Casey, Associated Press

BOSTON (AP) — Freeman Johnson, the oldest of the few remaining Pearl Harbor survivors, has died.

Johnson died Saturday at his home in Centerville, Massachusetts. He was 106, according to one of his daughters, Diane Johnson.

"It's going to be a hell of a Thanksgiving," said Diane Johnson, 72. "He's going to be up there with all of his friends and family and my mom."

Freeman Johnson was one of the estimated 87,000 military personnel on Oahu on Dec. 7, 1941, and was below deck working on a boiler of the USS St. Louis when the Japanese surprise attack happened. In a May 2026 interview with The Associated Press, Johnson said he didn't hear or see the attack. He never heard his shipmates firing anti-aircraft guns at the attacking planes — shooting down a torpedo plane.

"While all the rigamarole was going on topside, I was inside a steam drum. Couldn't see anything, absolutely nothing," said Johnson, whose job had been known as a firefighter on the ship.

Even as the St. Louis headed into the Pacific Ocean, Johnson knew little about the attack. By the time he was topside, the St. Louis, a light cruiser, had evaded midget submarines and safely set out to sea.

"We were way out to sea, way out. You couldn't see any land at all. All you saw was ocean," he said. "I was just a sailor, just a swabbie, I was not an officer. They don't tell you anything if you don't need to know. And I didn't need to know it. So they tell you nothing."

national.title: Third U.S. aircraft carrier in Middle East as Trump keeps options open in Iran war
national.summary: A third American aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East. A U.S. official speaking on the condition of anonymity on Monday confirmed the USS Theodore Roosevelt's arrival in the region.
national.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A third American aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East, a U.S. official said Monday, in a dramatic show of military might as President Donald Trump keeps his options open for next steps in the Iran war.

The U.S. official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military operations, confirmed the USS Theodore Roosevelt's arrival in the region.

It brings thousands of additional troops to the Middle East as Trump has oscillated between threatening additional large-scale strikes on Iran and insisting that the more than 8-month-old war "militarily is effectively over."

The Roosevelt, along with its accompanying strike force, left San Diego in September. It joins the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as smaller Navy ships, which are in the region to maintain a naval blockade of Iranian shipping.

The H.W. Bush arrived in the region in April, while the George Washington arrived in August. The Navy previously had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April, for the first time since 2003.

In addition to the three aircraft carriers, the flotilla in the Arabian Sea now includes 13 destroyers, two cruisers and a littoral combat ship, according to the Navy. Two more destroyers are in the Red Sea.

The Roosevelt had deployed along with the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group, which includes the USS John P. Murtha and USS Anchorage amphibious landing ships and around 2,000 Marines. Those ships have yet to make it to the region.

The third carrier arrived nearly two weeks after midterm elections that saw voters deliver major losses to Trump's Republican Party, driven in part by the unpopularity of the Iran war and its economic effects. The results led Vice President JD Vance to publicly break with Trump over the conflict, posting on social media that "the reason we lost is the war."

national.title: Tennessee names new corrections chief after botched executions
national.summary: Josh Smith has been appointed to lead the Department of Corrections in Tennessee following the botched execution of Christa Pike last month.
national.body: Josh Smith, who unexpectedly left his role as deputy director of the Bureau of Prisons in August, was appointed Monday to lead the Department of Corrections in Tennessee. Smith, a pardoned drug offender, was named to the position by Republican Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn."Josh brings a distinctive combination of executive leadership, firsthand correctional experience, and an understanding of the challenges facing our prison system," Blackburn said in her announcement. "He has demonstrated the ability to lead large organizations, make difficult decisions, and tackle longstanding problems."Smith said in a statement he is honored to have been selected. "Tennessee's correctional system faces significant challenges, including staffing shortages, institutional safety, and the need to strengthen leadership throughout the organization," he said. "I believe we can address these challenges by empowering our employees, establishing clear expectations, developing leaders, and maintaining an unwavering commitment to public safety."Smith is succeeding interim Director Christopher Hansen, who has been in office since Frank Strada resigned early last month following the botched execution of Christa Pike. Pike was the first female inmate scheduled to be executed by the state of Tennessee in 200 years. All executions following Pike's were stayed by Gov. Bill Lee. The lethal drug injection of pentobarbital left Pike on a ventilator with her arms blistered and bruised, her attorneys alleged. Her lawyers said in a court filing that Department of Corrections employees did not seem to realize that the IV was not placed correctly into Pike's veins, or that they were blown, allowing the lethal drug to enter her body. Pike's botched execution follows the failed execution of Tony Carruthers, who was set to be executed in May. Lee granted Carruthers a one-year reprieve after corrections staff spent more than an hour trying — and failing — to find a vein for the IV line for the lethal drug. Blackburn has called for the state to explore alternative means of execution, such as the electric chair. There are 40 inmates on death row in Tennessee.Smith was widely seen as an unconventional choice to serve as the No. 2 official at the Bureau of Prisons. Roblox is being sued by dozens of families and state attorneys general who claim online predators have been able to groom, extort and exploit kids they meet on the platform.The measure is being rolled out ahead of an inaugural congressional hearing Tuesday into the popular gaming portal. national.title: Trump administration moves to block China from indirect access to American AI tech
national.summary: The Trump administration has issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers.
national.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China's abilities to use U.S. chips to train their best artificial intelligence models.

The rule also was issued days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO amid scrutiny of his ties to a Chinese executive who used to lead Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which is suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls. The company provides computing power to Chinese companies using chips housed in Southeast Asian data centers, including facilities in Malaysia.

"The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Bureau of Industry and Security under the Commerce Department said in issuing the rule that took effect immediately.

Under the new rule, overseas data centers that serve companies in countries including China, Russia, Iran and Cuba are required to identify their end users. There also will be an additional, case-by-case licensing requirements for sales of chips for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil — countries that "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" to unauthorized destinations, the rule says.

The U.S. bans sales of the country's most advanced AI chips to China, seeking to maintain an edge in its rivalry with China for predominance in artificial intelligence. However, many lawmakers and policymakers believe the country's export control rules are not tough enough and filled with loopholes such as cloud computing that allow China to rent processing power built on American technology.

Last year, U.S. Rep. Michael Lawler, a New York Republican, introduced a bill to broaden the U.S. export controls to include remote access. He told Congress "physical export controls" under current rules do not apply to remote access, allowing China to "access our tech through the cloud" and giving it "a real tool to sidestep" U.S. export restrictions. The bill has passed the House.

national.title: U.S. tightens controls on remote access to AI technology amid Nvidia fallout
national.summary: The new rule closes a loophole that existed that allowed Chinese companies to still access advanced AI chips remotely, despite U.S. restrictions on their physical sale to China.
national.body:
The U.S. government has announced a rule to prevent remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips and servers, closing a loophole that could let adversarial governments access American AI technology through overseas data centers.

Technology Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang steps down amid alleged spy scandal The move comes amid the fallout at Nvidia, the world's dominant producer of AI chips, following revelations that CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials suspected of being a Chinese intelligence operative. NPR has not independently verified the claims. Huang stepped down as CEO last week.

Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, is a former executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data center company. Jensen Huang has personally lobbied President Trump to loosen restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China. It is not known if Alice Huang influenced this activity.

U.S. vs. China: Inside a great power rivalry Trump administration backs off Nvidia H20 chip crackdown after Mar-a-Lago dinner The rapid advancement in cloud computing and AI infrastructure has made it possible to access advanced U.S. computing capabilities remotely, including through data centers located outside countries subject to U.S. export restrictions, the U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) said in a statement on Monday.

The rule is designed to reinforce existing restrictions on access to sensitive American AI technology through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in other countries, which could threaten national security

However, a loophole existed where Chinese companies could still access those chips remotely, despite U.S. restrictions on their physical sale to China.

"The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten U.S. national security," the BIS statement said.

The government refers to artificial intelligence as "super intelligence" following an executive order signed by President Trump in September.

national.body: Robert Pattinson is the new 007. After rampant online speculation about who would take over the iconic spy character from Daniel Craig, the franchise announced Monday that Pattinson will be the next James Bond. Pattinson only entered the rumor mill recently after the revelation that he screen-tested for the role, the Associated Press reported, along with a few other finalists."Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey," Villeneuve said in a statement. "We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin."Pattinson is already associated with three mega-franchises: "The Batman," "Twilight" and "Harry Potter."Since his breakthrough in "Twilight," Pattinson has also worked in more independent films such as "Good Time," "The Lighthouse" and "Mickey 17." Maria Sherman, Associated Press Maria Sherman, Associated Press

NEW YORK (AP) — Call her a Raye of sunshine. The English singer-songwriter leads the 2027 Grammy Award nominations, the Recording Academy announced Monday.

Raye is up for 11 awards at February's ceremony: record, song and album of the year — the first time she's been nominated in those big categories — as well as songwriter of the year non-classical, a variety of pop categories and music video.

Her 11 nods also mean she has tied Beyoncé's record at the 2025 Grammys for the most nominations in a single year by a female artist.

Speaking of Bey: She continues her reign as the most-nominated artist in Grammy history, scoring her 100th nod for "Morning Dew (Donk)" in the R&B solo performance category.

Raye, who is riding the success of her critically acclaimed album "This Music May Contain Hope," has 15 Grammy nominations across her career. She's never won one, though she was previously recognized by the Recording Academy with the noncompetitive Harry Belafonte best song for social change award.

Spanish singer Rosalía, fresh off her album of the year win at the 27th annual Latin Grammy Awards on Thursday for her avant-garde "Lux," follows Raye with nine nominations. She's a first-time nominee in all the categories she's up for: record, song and album of the year as well as pop solo performance, alternative music performance, alternative music album, Latin song, global music performance and music video.

Following her are Miranda Lambert, Olivia Rodrigo, Phoebe Bridgers and first-time nominee Ella Langley, who are tied with seven nods each.

national.body: Washington — President Trump said he "would not mind" seeing Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO of Nvidia, after he resigned last week amid allegations of two affairs. The president said he doesn't know if Alice Huang, one of the women allegedly involved with Jensen Huang, was a Chinese spy. "I would not mind. And just before the president left, the Trump administration announced a new rule that's intended to curb efforts by China to bypass the restrictions by remotely accessing the chips through data centers in third countries. The president also dismissed concerns that Alice Huang may be spying for China. She's a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a former gaming company that is now an AI infrastructure and cloud computing company and is one of Nvidia's biggest foreign customers."Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy," Mr. Trump said. Elon Musk, tech executives and Nvidia employees have signed a petition calling for Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia. national.title: U.N. talks seek to rein in 'killer robots' as fears over AI weapons grow
national.summary: Countries are meeting in Geneva to negotiate rules on weapons that can select and kill targets without human intervention. But with the U.S., Russia and Israel resisting legally binding controls, campaigners fear the window to act is closing.
national.body:
GENEVA — Negotiations on possible rules for the use of lethal autonomous weapons, also known as 'killer robots' are underway at the United Nations in Geneva.

Supporters of controls on autonomous weapons say this week's U.N. conference on Certain Conventional Weapons (or CCW), which meets just once every five years, is the last best chance to agree rules before it is too late.

Warfare technology has advanced rapidly in the last few years, with some experts warning that the world is just months away from having weapons that can choose targets and make the decision to kill autonomously.

In Ukraine and Gaza, AI-assisted weapons have already been used to take out targets, with Ukrainian civilians reporting being 'hunted' by drones as they shop or go to school. But these are still controlled remotely by humans.

Humanitarian organizations say the decision to kill – and responsibility for that choice – must stay in human hands. Ahead of this week's meeting, the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross and the Pope have all called for legally binding rules. U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned that allowing fully autonomous weapons to kill would be 'crossing a moral red line'.

The Red Cross is especially worried that existing rules of war – the Geneva Conventions – cannot be fully respected by autonomous weapons. War is often chaotic and confusing, and the situation can change rapidly. Under the Conventions, soldiers who are wounded or in the process of surrendering can no longer be targeted.

Georgia Haines, a legal adviser with the Red Cross, worries that autonomous weapons will not be able to distinguish between a soldier who is still fighting, one who is wounded and one who wants to surrender.

'The risk is that, based on the technology we are seeing, they are not able to understand in the same way that a human is the contextual signals. And so the risks are incredibly high that there will be a misidentification of a target.'

national.title: The Nvidia scandal is heightening America's AI rivalry with China ahead of Trump's visit
national.summary: Well before reports emerged that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, the advanced chips made by his company were at the center of the race between the U.S. and China to dominate artificial intelligence.
national.body:
HONG KONG (AP) — Well before reports emerged that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, the advanced chips made by his company were at the center of the race between the U.S. and China to dominate artificial intelligence.

As President Donald Trump prepares to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week in China, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle in Congress are seizing on the affair to press for tighter restrictions on technology exports to protect America's edge.

"The scandal, in many ways, encapsulates the rivalry, where concerns around national security, export control, and foreign policy get intertwined," said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst at London-based technology research and advisory group Omdia.

At the heart of the competition to build the most advanced artificial intelligence is the race to access the most powerful AI chips. U.S.-led restrictions have barred China from getting the world's most advanced AI chips, a strategy that has led Beijing to accuse the U.S. of pursuing an AI monopoly.

Once commanding some 95% of market share in China, Nvidia's sales to China have plummeted due to the export restrictions, first applied during the Biden administration. After Huang lobbied Washington to loosen the limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China, Trump earlier this year greenlighted the export of its highly-advanced, though not the most powerful, H200 chips.

Trump has spoken admiringly of Huang — a man at the center of the AI boom Trump has been keen to promote — and the two have talked regularly during his second term, including at least twice this week as the scandal grew around the tech executive.

The strategy in Washington has been largely focused on hardware, with officials believing if they controlled where California-based Nvidia's best chips go, they'd be in control of the race for the most capable AI, said Shaoyu Yuan, an assistant professor at New York University's Center for Global Affairs.

That strategy was effective in slowing down Chinese companies, Yuan said, but it assumed the primary threat was the physical hardware, not access to leaders like Huang.

Flights across the US were returning to normal levels, after a weekend of disruption as the national air-traffic control system recovered from a technical failure that prompted a rare national ground stop.

More than 2,500 flights into or out of the US were delayed and 325 flights cancelled on Monday morning, a significant drop from the thousands delayed and cancelled on Friday, according to the latest data from FlightAware. , external

"What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack," President Donald Trump said on Monday.

Asked by reporters if he took any responsibility for the ground stop, Trump said he did not.

"I don't take any responsibility," Trump said, praising his officials. "They did a great job, Secretary Duffy, acted incredibly."

national.title: Commerce Department moves to curb remote access to AI chips
national.summary: U.S. announces a temporary rule to limit foreign countries' access to advanced chips via data centers in other countries.
national.body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security on Monday issued an interim rule limiting other countries' access to advanced chips that power artificial intelligence.The federal government is stepping up scrutiny of semiconductor exports to ensure that such shipments don't bypass existing regulations prohibiting their sale to certain U.S. competitors, such as China. The temporary regulations follow last week's shock resignation of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, as well as a subordinate at the company. Huang's exit has heightened concerns that China and other nations could access Nvidia's advanced chips by renting computing resources through data centers in Southeast Asia. "The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) said in a statement on Monday. "The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten U.S. national security."In addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, the new rule will require licenses for exporting, re-exporting, or transferring advanced semiconductors to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore or Thailand. national.title: Preliminary study finds a clue in the quest to help diagnose CTE in the living
national.summary: Scientists stumbled onto a hint that measuring a toxic protein tied to Alzheimer's disease just might one day be useful in diagnosing a different brain disease in football players and others who have suffered repeated blows to the head.
national.body:
Lauran Neergaard, Associated Press Lauran Neergaard, Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — Scientists stumbled onto a hint that measuring a toxic protein tied to Alzheimer's disease just might one day be useful in diagnosing a different brain disease in football players and others who have suffered repeated blows to the head.

Doctors evaluate symptoms such as mood swings and memory loss to try to tell if patients may have CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, a disease linked to concussions and other brain trauma. But other diseases cause similar symptoms, and a CTE diagnosis can only be confirmed by examining the brain after death.

The new clue involves a protein called tau that normally supports neurons but becomes abnormal in Alzheimer's, tangling inside those nerve cells. Researchers at Washington University in St. Louis were using autopsy samples to study a tau fragment called eMTBR-tau243 that may help track those tangles when they found something unusual: a patient with high levels of that biomarker even though records showed the person didn't have Alzheimer's but advanced CTE instead.

The researchers turned to a larger collection of autopsied brain and other samples, and eventually tested blood stored from 11 people who had been classified as having CTE.

WATCH: New study reveals widespread signs of brain trauma among former NFL players

Compared to healthy people, levels of eMTBR-tau243 were higher in those with advanced CTE, said study coauthor Chihiro Sato, a WashU assistant neurology professor. That biomarker couldn't reliably identify early-stage CTE.

It is an interesting but very preliminary finding, requiring far larger studies to see if there is a real connection, cautioned Dr. Rudolph Castellani, a neuropathologist at Northwestern University who wasn't involved with the research.

national.body:
Steven Grattan, Associated Press Steven Grattan, Associated Press

MEXICO CITY (AP) — A coalition of countries seeking to accelerate the global transition away from fossil fuels is preparing to unveil new national plans at the ongoing United Nations climate talks, known as COP31, in Antalya, Turkey, pressing ahead despite the withdrawal of Colombia, one of its founding members.

The coalition, launched in the Colombian coastal city of Santa Marta in April, is expected to release a progress report this week outlining steps taken by participating countries, including additional national plans to reduce dependence on coal, oil and gas.

The announcement comes as Ireland and the Pacific island nation of Tuvalu prepare to take over leadership of the initiative from Colombia and the Netherlands, with a second international conference planned for July 2027.

A statement from Ireland's Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment confirmed Colombia's withdrawal and said preparations were well advanced for a program of events in both countries next year. Neither the Environment Ministry nor the presidential office responded to questions about Colombia's withdrawal or its plans to attend the next conference.

"This process is bigger than any one country," the department said, adding that further details would be announced at a formal handover during COP31.

The Santa Marta conference emerged from frustration over the slow pace of international efforts to reduce dependence on coal, oil and gas, the fossil fuels that are the main drivers of global warming.

The initiative brought representatives from 57 countries together to explore ways of turning international commitments to move away from fossil fuels, the main drivers of global warming, into concrete national policies. Unlike formal U.N. climate negotiations, the gathering was designed to encourage open discussions without pressure to reach binding agreements or commit to specific deadlines.

national.title: Lindsay Clancy to face a new trial in spring of 2027 over children's killing
national.summary: A new trial is set in Massachusetts against Lindsay Clancy as prosecutors seek a criminal conviction over the killing of her three young children.
national.body:
Prosecutors are seeking a new trial for Lindsay Clancy in the deaths of her three children. The trial is scheduled to begin on March 29, 2027.

There had been speculation that the mistrial of her first trial might spur prosecutors to consider lesser charges that wouldn't require a jury, such as manslaughter or second-degree murder. But no changes to the charges were made in Monday's court hearing.

"Given what the charges are, it requires a jury trial," Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague told Judge William Sullivan in Plymouth, Mass.

In response, Clancy's defense attorney Kevin Reddington stated, "I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury, that it's an indirect comment from the DA that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments."

Consider This from NPR The Lindsay Clancy case ends in a mistrial. Where might it go from here? Judge Sullivan is expected to preside over the new trial. He oversaw Clancy's murder trial that ended in a mistrial two months ago.

The decision to retry Clancy emerges after the judge denied a request from Clancy's defense team to dismiss the criminal charges against her on double jeopardy grounds.

Clancy's defense has argued that she shouldn't be held criminally responsible for killing her young children because she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis.

Clancy was initially tried on three charges of first-degree murder, one for each of her children. Her case has drawn intense media interest, due to the shocking killings of her young children. And as WBUR has reported , the trial has also sparked conspiracy theories online.

national.title: Five EU countries announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda
national.summary: Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands have announced a "return hub" for failed asylum seekers.
national.body:
Five EU countries will open a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda next year as part of a broader push to boost removals.

Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to open a "return hub" ready to accept transfers in 2027, the Dutch and Danish governments announced in statements.

The countries said the scheme would apply to migrants staying illegally in their nations who are subject to deportation, with the Dutch government adding it will provide an alternative if deportees cannot be returned to their country of origin.

Deportees will be able to either integrate into Rwandan society or return to their home country, the nations said.

The scheme will apply to people who have exhausted their legal avenues to stay in the five nations - unlike a scrapped British deal that envisaged sending people to Rwanda to have their claims processed. Legal challenges meant the UK deal never took off, and it was eventually junked by the incoming Labour government in 2024 .

Downing Street has not ruled out the UK joining the scheme, saying they will watch it "with interest".

The five countries say the plan to send migrants abroad is in line with EU and international law, but human rights bodies say it could violate migrant rights.

The deal follows a recent EU reform that allowed for the creation of hubs outside of the bloc.

BRUSSELS (AP) — European Union countries on Monday accused Russia of trying to drag out talks on ending the war in Ukraine while it bombs power plants and other infrastructure to make life even harder for civilians as winter closes in.

The bloc also imposed sanctions on nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions, and targeted several businesspeople with links to the energy sector, the trade in oil and petroleum products. It slapped asset freezes and travel bans on dozens of others accused of spreading pro-Russian propaganda and disinformation.

At talks in Brussels, EU foreign ministers said the priority in Ukraine should be to secure a ceasefire and then a real peace agreement. They said that Russia started the nearly five-year war and must back down rather than make fresh demands of Ukraine and its Western supporters.

"Let's not blur the picture right now. What we need to see is a ceasefire," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said before chairing the meeting. "We don't see it at the moment. We see that Russia is really escalating."

After negotiations in Abu Dhabi last week, the United States encouraged Ukraine and its backers to agree to a Russian demand for a new security framework for Europe, suggesting that it might help bring peace.

But the Europeans see that as a Russian attempt to weaken NATO by obliging the military alliance to pull troops and equipment back westward, similar to the way they were deployed before the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland joined in 1999.

That demand is "really absurd," Kallas said. "If we look at the history, none of these countries has ever attacked Russia." She said Russia's tactic is always to demand more even though "they started the war. They are the aggressor. And there's one victim."

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said: "Europe has a security architecture – we don't need a new one, we just need respect from everyone for the existing security architecture." He said that is "the foundation for any conceivable agreement, from the European point of view."

In Boston, Lincolnshire, a supplier of ready meals to Marks & Spencer (M&S) manufactures thousands of portions of spaghetti bolognese to be sent to the retailer's shops in the Republic of Ireland.

Every truck full of food sent to European Union countries requires hundreds of pages of forms, checks by vets, expense and delays.

It has cost M&S millions of pounds and is part of that reason the British business shut down 11 French stores in 2021.

Many smaller exporters stopped sending their goods to the EU entirely. Some produce, including sausages and certain types of seafood, were entirely stopped.

All this was the predictable consequence of former Prime Minister Boris Johnson’s 2020 deal prioritising regulatory freedom over freeflowing goods trade.

Ukraine has scaled up its long-range aerial assaults on Russia, as well as the illegally annexed Crimean Peninsula and the Black and the Azov seas, with more than 1,000 drones used in some daily attacks in recent months.

In the Rostov region near the border with Ukraine, three people in the city of Azov were wounded by drones, Gov. Yuri Slyusar said.

JOHANNESBURG (AP) — At least 17 people were killed in two mass shootings on the same day in South Africa. Motives have not been immediately established for the crimes some 530 kilometers (330 miles) apart, police said Monday.

Eight people were found dead inside a bullet-riddled vehicle in Sweetwaters, outside the city of Pietermaritzburg, according to police, who said they had not immediately identified the victims or any suspects in the shooting Sunday.

Nine people were found dead with gunshot wounds inside a shack in the informal settlement of Jeffsville near South Africa's capital, Pretoria. The shooting reportedly took place Sunday night and no arrests have been made.

The Jeffsville case is being investigated by the serious and violent crimes, murder and robbery unit in Gauteng province.

The incident is reported to have occurred between 10 p.m. and 11 p.m., police said.

"Police were alerted at approximately 07:30 this morning, 16 November 2026. On arrival, members found the bodies of nine people, six males and three females, inside the four-roomed shack with gunshot wounds," said police spokesperson Brenda Muridili.

Gauteng Police Commissioner Tommy Mthombeni said the killings could be related to a previous shooting at a nearby informal settlement in Saulsville last year where 12 people were killed and 13 injured.

local.title: FAA: L3Harris router in Arkansas sparked nationwide ground stop
local.summary: The router is currently under evaluation at an L3Harris lab in Florida. L3Harris is one of Rochester's largest employers.
local.body:
The nationwide ground stop of all planes in the country on Friday was caused by an L3Harris router in El Dorado, Arkansas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.

Headquartered in Melbourne, Florida, L3Harris is one of the largest defense and communications contractors in the country, employing about 45,000 people — including roughly 3,800 in the Rochester area. The company is one of the region's largest employers.

Along with manufacturing tactical radio and satellite technology, L3 Harris plays a major role in managing federal communication systems.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is seeking billions of dollars from Congress for a new network built “by the best companies in the world, including AT&T, Verizon and Lumens,” Duffy told NBC News' "Meet the Press."

“I want to get away from L3Harris and get to a new one, but they own the network. I can’t cancel the network that they own,” he said.

The router L3Harris installed began "broadcasting all of this data into our network," which ultimately led the FAA to ground all commercial planes in the country Friday afternoon. The router, he added, is being examined at an L3Harris lab in Florida.

"We have to unwind, was this a technical install error or was this an issue in the install itself," Duffy said, in a Sunday interview with CNN's Dana Bash.

The FAA says the router caused "instability" at 17 of the nation's 22 air traffic control centers.

local.title: Children can wait months for autism screening. UR cut the delay. Then funding ran out
local.summary: University of Rochester Medicine has been bringing autism evaluations directly to underserved families. But a lack of federal funding is preventing longevity and expansion.
local.body:
Listen • 2:25 After teachers complained about their frequent behavioral issues, Niya Walters was desperate to get her 5-year-old twins evaluated and diagnosed.

But URochester Medicine Developmental and Behavioral Pediatrics said there was a nine- to 12-month wait list to get her kids assessed.

"I didn't know if I wanted to go through with it," Walters said. "Because I was looking for something now. I knew they needed help now."

Walters later caught a break when she received a call from the Rochester City School District's director of special education who told her that URochester Medicine would be doing evaluations at Mary McLeod Bethune School No. 45 for a limited time under the EACH ( Every Child's Access to Care and Health ) Youth Initiative. It was a novel project that officials said aimed at "accelerating access to developmental services for underserved families."

Walter completed the application, and her kids were seen within a week.

"I know that without the diagnosis it was like a dead end," Walter said. "I'm just trying to see what else they have in store for them, so I can get them on board."

Both twins left the appointment with an official diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder. And Walters left relieved. She knew the diagnoses meant more resources and better support for her children.

"It was almost like having a golden ticket into a world of their own," Walters said. "A world that they would feel more comfortable in."

This year marked Brooks-TLC Hospital’s ninth year participating in Roc
local.body:
Brooks-TLC Hospital System employees came together to make a difference in the community, collecting a record-breaking total of more than 1,170 food items during the 21st annual Rock Out Hunger food drive benefiting FeedMore WNY.

This year marked Brooks-TLC Hospital's ninth year participating in Rock Out Hunger as part of Kaleida Health's involvement in the annual food drive, which brings organizations and community partners together to help address food insecurity throughout Western New York.

Donations collected by Brooks-TLC Hospital will support FeedMore WNY partner organizations serving local communities in Chautauqua County, including the Boys and Girls Club of Northern Chautauqua County, Chautauqua County Rural Ministries Friendly Kitchen, Dunkirk City Schools 3 and 7, Dunkirk Conference Center, The Dunkirk Salvation Army, St. Elizabeth Ann Seton Food Closet and Dunkirk Middle and High School.

"We are proud to be part of Rock Out Hunger and grateful for the opportunity to give back to the communities we serve," said Ken Morris, president, Brooks-TLC Hospital. "The generosity and enthusiasm demonstrated by our employees are proof to the commitment they have not only to providing exceptional care, but also to supporting our neighbors beyond the walls of our hospital. Every donation makes a difference and we are proud to see our team come together for such an important cause."

Adding a little friendly competition to this year's food drive, 11 departments across the organization participated in a department-versus-department challenge to collect the most food items and decorate their own shopping carts. The competition brought creativity and team spirit to the initiative, with departments transforming shopping carts into festive displays while filling them with food donations.

Together, employees filled more than eight shopping carts with food, setting a new collection record for Brooks-TLC Hospital's participation in the program.

The donations come at an important time for families throughout the region. According to the 2025 Chautauqua County Community Health Assessment, approximately 15% of county residents experience food insecurity, compared to 13% statewide and 14% nationally. Food insecurity can be especially challenging in rural communities, where transportation barriers, fewer grocery options and long distances to food assistance programs can make accessing nutritious food more difficult.

local.title: What happened to the hundreds of asylum seekers NY sent to Rochester?
local.summary: Through the state's Migrant Relocation Assistance Program 178 families eventually relocated to Monroe Country, receiving help with housing and other services as they worked to become self-sufficient, although some left.
local.body:
Listen • 1:42 A state-run program created to relocate asylum seekers out of crowded New York City shelters in 2023 ended up assisting 671 families numbering more than 2,000 adults and children.

Roughly half of those went to two places: Albany and Rochester. The majority came to Rochester, their journey beginning with a bus ride that brought them to a downtown hotel .

Three years later, both the program and the hotel have been shut down. And officials estimate that more than a quarter of the people who came to Rochester have left, returning to New York City, moving elsewhere or leaving the country.

The families were mainly from Central and South America, with some individuals from Haiti and parts of Africa.

They left for a variety of reasons, including limited job opportunities, or fear of being more vulnerable to immigration enforcement in a mid-sized city versus New York City. And there were delays in receiving work authorization, meaning they couldn’t afford to stay, said Daisy Ruiz-Marin, community response lead at Rochester's Ibero-American Action League, which oversaw the state’s Migrant Relocation Assistance Program locally.

"Some folks decided to return back to a New York City shelter,” she said, “because even though Monroe County is more affordable at the time of their graduation (from the state program), there was no way for them to continue being self-sufficient for their family, so they ended up deciding to relocate."

But many have stayed, including a family of three from Nicaragua.

The mother and father found work in retail, while the child enrolled in school — making a home in a city that the mother said she remembers feeling was small and developing when they first arrived.

local.title: Family at home can be big help for deer hunters
local.summary: Families across Western New York are getting ready for two familiar signs of the season: winter weather and the opening of New York’s Southern Zone big game hunting season this coming Saturday. While some families have watched their children grow up and leave the nest, others are just introducing th
local.body:
Families across Western New York are getting ready for two familiar signs of the season: winter weather and the opening of New York’s Southern Zone big game hunting season this coming Saturday.

While some families have watched their children grow up and leave the nest, others are just introducing their youngsters to the traditions of deer hunting. In many households, both mom and dad hunt. In others, mom is the one taking the kids into the woods. Either way, hunting season has a way of bringing families together in any number of ways.

Family members who are not heading out with a hunting license and blaze orange can help make Opening Day special too. The home-stay family may be among the most important members of the Opening Day support crew.

They know that the night before Opening Day is no time to discover that someone’s gloves have disappeared, the flashlight needs batteries or the hunting boots are still sitting in the garage with a sack of spider webs that made a winter home. Hunters almost always need help to check clothing, licenses, required safety equipment, snack supplies, water and other essentials. A thermos of hot coffee or cocoa can earn the home-family honorary family MVP status.

Hunters heading out before daylight, 3:30 a.m. come early, and hunters appreciate a good breakfast. Something warm, filling and easy to eat is a welcome start. Just remember, they don't need a three-course meal when they’re trying to get into the woods before sunrise, just wholesome protein.

Check the forecast, remind their hunters to dress in layers (or not), and make sure they’re prepared for changing conditions. November in Western New York can deliver sunshine, freezing temperatures, rain, snow and wind, sometimes before lunchtime!

Remind everyone to wear the required fluorescent orange or pink clothing, handle firearms responsibly, identify their target and what lies beyond it, and follow all hunting regulations. Firearms should always be unloaded when being transported, and every hunter should know where their companions are once they head for the forest. A responsible hunter never takes a shot unless absolutely certain it is safe. Look beyond the target.

Know where everyone plans to hunt, when they expect to return, and how they can be reached. If plans change, make sure someone at home knows. Never let a hunter feel pressured to take an unsafe shot or stay in dangerous weather just to keep up with expectations.

local.body:
QUEENSBURY -- One year can make quite a difference and for Clymer/Sherman/Panama's Savannah Whitney it meant being a whole minute faster and jumping from 39th to 14th overall in the New York State Public High School Athletic Association Class C cross country championships at Queensbury High School on Saturday afternoon. The Wolfpack eighth-grader posted a time of 19:03.4 to claim 14th overall in the Class C race, while the winning time was posted by Bronxville sophomore Mia Horgan at 17:40.9 to retain her championship.

Horgan's time was not enough to help Bronxville repeat with the team title as Section VIII's Cold Spring Harbor posted the low score of 58.

In the Class D race, the Frewsburg girls finished sixth with a team score of 173, while Section III's South Lewis claimed the team title at 48.

The Bears were led by senior Grace Gilevski taking 21st in team points and 46th overall at 20:46.8, junior Raegan Cheney came 25th in team and 51st overall at 21:02.2, freshman Skye Carter posted 34 team points and 69th overall at 21:37.3, seventh-grader Alina Whippo ran to 46th team points and 90th overall at 22:54.1, eighth-grader Greta Gilevski was 47th in team and 91st overall at 22:56.9, senior Olivia Nelson ran to 93rd overall at 23:08.2 and sophomore Alexis Darling took 95th at 23:18.8.

Qualifying as an individual, Maple Grove junior Lily Elliss posted the best local time in the Class D race, running a sub-20 time of 19:55.0 to take 28th overall.

local.body:
DRYDEN -- After getting out of the Section VI tournament as the Class C champion it was smooth sailing for Wilson and the Lakewomen outscored opponents 12-1 in the New York State Public High School Athletic Association championships to claim the program's first state title at a perfect 21-0-0 on Sunday at Dryden High School.

Wilson was up against Section V's Kendall in the Far West Regionals a week ago and it took just over a minute for the Lakewomen to get all they needed to advance. Zoey Beck scored from Lilly Gurski in the second minute and Lucy Madan added an insurance goal from Gurski again in the 60th minute while Brooke Urban needed just three saves for the 2-0 clean sheet.

Things only got easier in the state semifinals as Wilson cruised past Section X's St. Lawrence 7-1 at Moravia High School on Saturday. Junior forward Addison Elia put on a show as she scored four goals in the contest, eighth-grader Macaela Boyer provided two goals and an assist, Abigail Labarre scored once and Gurski, Kyra Fellows and Kairi Beck had two assists each.

Wilson remained tied at halftime with Section II's Stillwater, but Gurski struck first and the Lakewomen added two more to secure the first girls soccer state title in Section VI since Allegany-Limestone won in 2017.

MIDDLETOWN -- Section VI also brought home a title for the boys as Lewiston-Porter dominated the Class A competition, outscoring opponents 16-1 in four NYSPHSAA games to secure the first title in program history.

The Lancers made it the second year in a row for Section VI taking home the Class A title, following up East Aurora last season.

Lewiston-Porter first won its subregional against Section V's Pittsford Sutherland 2-0 courtesy of goals by Luke and Wyatt Leardini, then in a subregional match against Section IV's Maine-Endwell the Lancers received four goals from Luke Leardini in a dominant 7-1 win.

The Lancers did not slow down once they got to Middletown High School on Friday, first defeating Section II's Averill Park 4-0 and then on Saturday night they shut out Section III's Jamesville-DeWitt 3-0.

local.body:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. (AP) -- Geno Smith left the game, came back and then left again -- this time, for good.

Now, Aaron Glenn and the struggling New York Jets have a serious quarterback question as they take a five-game skid to Los Angeles to face the winless Chargers next week.

An ankle injury knocked Smith out of the Jets’ 32-12 loss to the Buffalo Bills in the third quarter Sunday after he missed a series to start the second half to be evaluated for a head injury. Rookie Cade Klubnik stepped in for Smith both times, and could be pressed into making his first NFL start if the veteran can’t go next Sunday.

The Jets also have Will Levis, a second-round pick of Tennessee in 2023, on the practice squad.

Glenn was uncertain if Smith and rookie wide receiver Omar Cooper Jr., who left after the Jets’ first offensive play, had high ankle sprains.

“I don’t know,” Glenn said. “I just know they’re both ankles right now. I’ll end up getting that information sometime next week.”

Smith was 13 of 21 for 148 yards. Klubnik was 11 of 20 for 137 yards with an interception, and ran three times for 26 yards. He was also sacked three times.

“Man, this was as tough as it gets for any young quarterback to go against this front that really does a good job of rushing the passer,” Glenn said. “But just from the naked eye, I thought he did a pretty good job.”

SOUTH DAYTON -- The Pine Valley Central School District Board of Education invites qualified district residents interested in serving local students, schools, and the community to apply for a Board seat vacancy created by a resignation.

The Board intends to fill the vacancy by appointment. The selected appointee will serve from January until the next regular school district election on May 18, 2027.

Board of Education members serve without compensation and help guide the district's educational priorities, policies, and responsible use of resources. Appointees must be prepared to attend Board meetings, review meeting materials, participate in required training, maintain legally required confidentiality, and work collaboratively in the interests of all district students. A commitment to public education, thoughtful decision-making, and responsible financial oversight is encouraged.

To be eligible for appointment – which will be verified prior to selection – applicants must meet the following criteria:

-- Have been a continuous district resident for at least one year before taking office.

-- Not be employed by the Board of Education on which they would serve.

-- Not reside in the same household with a family member serving on the same Board.

-- Not have been removed from a school district office within the preceding year.

entertainment.body:
Billboard’ Live Music Summit presented by VENU, brought the live entertainment industry together at the 1 Hotel West Hollywood on Nov. 10 for a celebration of the artists, executives and innovators shaping the future of touring. The festivities began the evening before, when VENU® hosted its Money & Music Cocktail Hour at The Sunrose in West Hollywood. The event set the stage for conversations about the changing business of live entertainment. It included an intimate fireside chat with J.W. Roth, Founder, Chairman and CEO of VENU, and Ron Bension, former President and CEO of ASM Global, veteran entertainment executive and strategic advisor to VENU, moderated by Billboard co-chief content officer Jason Lipshutz.

VENU’s Disruptor Award also returned for its second year recognizing the visionaries challenging convention and creating new possibilities for live entertainment. .

Presented by VENU’s Founder, Chairman and CEO, J.W. Roth, the honor went to Jorge Juárez, CEO of Westwood Entertainment and founder of Novus Media, whose work has helped propel Música Mexicana onto some of the world’s most prominent stages.

If you were a British actor and 6’0 or above you were bound to be given some consideration for this role. (Tough luck, Tom Holland.)

Pattison will be joined by Denis Villeneuve, director of the Dune trilogy (the upcoming Dune 3 flick will star Pattison) and Arrival . He joins as the Bond franchise enters a new era, with Amazon MGM taking control of the beloved series for its 26th official outing, after decades under the stewardship of the Broccoli family and producer Michael Wilson.

Now comes the fun part: the Bond song. Nearly all of the movies has been soundtracked with a signature, original song for its opening credit sequence, a tradition that began with Shirley Bassey ’s iconic “Goldfinger” from 1964.

Music’s finest has since tackled the mission with chart success , to boot. Duran Duran ’s “A View to Kill” is the only Bond song to hit No. 1 on Billboard’s Hot 100 , with Carly Simon (1977’s “Nobody Does it Better,” No. 2), Paul McCartney (1973’s “Live and Let Die,” No. 2) and Sheena Easton (1981’s “For Your Eyes Only,” No. 4) also scoring big hits with their own themes. In the 21st century, Adele (2012’s “Skyfall,” No. 8), Madonna (“Die Another Day,” No. 8), and Billie Eilish (“No Time to Die,” No. 16) have all also seen similar success.

For many it’s a dream gig, and the ultimate collaboration between music and a film series that prides itself on being the coolest and suavest of them all. These are our frontrunner predictions for who will record the title track to the upcoming 26th James Bond film, presented in no particular order.

Callum Turner, Dua’s husband, was reportedly part of the final five actors that were in consideration for the role, making it a distinct possibility that the pair could pull off a remarkable double-act. Ultimately Turner was passed over, but Dua’s name has still been floated as a potential future Bond performer. She has an international profile, and her 2024 live album recorded at the Royal Albert Hall showed her ability to perform with a string section, undoubtedly a prerequisite for cutting a track for the franchise. – THOMAS SMITH

entertainment.body:

"You know, I wonder though how far we can take her now, because if you look out in the world, there are a lot of Sue Sylvesters out there,” Lynch mused. “I think I kind of made the mold for everybody, but I can’t wait. Though it remains to be seen which of the cast—which also included Matthew Morrison , Harry Shum Jr. , Lea Michele , Chris Colfer , Amber Riley and more—will appear in the reboot, creator Ryan Murphy previously hinted that some William McKinley High School alums will be returning.

"I've been in touch with around 10 of the original cast members," he told Entertainment Tonight in September. "It's very sweet, and they all had a lot of questions, but they all were very enthusiastic about the idea."

Michele had also expressed interest in playing Rachel Berry again in a potential Glee revival—if it felt right.

entertainment.title: Shakira Goes Global, Drake Gets Love, and More Latin Music Takeaways from the 2027 Grammy Nominations
entertainment.summary: One of the biggest genres in the U.S. saw interesting — and confusing — Grammy nods
entertainment.body:
The Recording Academy doesn’t always get it right when it comes to Latin music, but lately they’ve been trying. Last year, voters from the Latin Recording Academy were able to cast ballots in the standard edition, making for a more diverse voting pool. It’s a move that’s already paid off. Earlier this year, at the 2026 awards, Bad Bunny made history with the first Album of the Year win for a full Spanish-language album. Now, with the 2027 Grammy nominations , one of the biggest genres in the U.S. is still front and center — even if some of the nods are perplexing. Let’s take a look at all of the Latin music highlights from this year’s nominations.

Rosalía just made history at the Latin Grammys when she became the first woman to win Album of the Year three times. Now, the Spanish singer is the second-most-decorated nominee for the 2027 Grammys, and she could follow Bad Bunny’s lead with another historic AOTY win. If Rosalía’s Lux snags the highest honor of the night, she would become the first woman to win in the category with a Spanish-language project.

There were a handful of Latin music first-time nominees across categories. Ryan Castro secured two nods in the Best Música Urbana Album, one for his solo LP Hopi Sendé and another for his collaborative album with J Balvin, Omerta . Meanwhile, Argentine musician Milo J earned recognition in the Best Latin Song and Best Latin Rock or Alternative Album categories for his Latin Grammy-winning project La vida era Más Corta. Venezuelan American singer Elena Rose also received her first-ever Grammy nod, in the Best Latin Pop Album category. About that…

… Rose’s nomination leads us to the unfortunate catch-all that the Best Latin Pop Album category became this year. As we said, the Academy doesn’t always get it right when it comes to Latin music. Nowhere is that more blatant than this category, which is jam-packed with an array of popular Latin artists who make distinct music from each other. Karol G’s alternative album No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto makes some sense here, as does Mon Laferte’s Femme Fatale — but Carín León’s Muda runs the gamut of genres from norteño to salsa and soul. It makes no sense here, and Rawayana’s and Elena Rose’s genre-bending albums don’t really, either. Rather than find a way to honor these impressive works and the widely varied Latin genres they’re pushing forward, the Academy seems to be stuffing them under one confusing umbrella. entertainment.title: C. Tangana & Spanish Rap Collective Agorazein Move Madrid 10 Years Later With Its Return: ‘This Is Our Legacy’
entertainment.summary: The lyrical troupe that helped introduce “El Madrileño” is bringing back the songs and style of its early days for four shows at Movistar Arena.
entertainment.body:
Before his acclaimed 2021 album El Madrileño , arena tours and his directorial debut with the documentary La Guitarra Flamenca de Yerai Cortés (2024), C. Tangana was part of Agorazein, the rap collective he formed with a group of friends in Madrid. It was where he first started making a name for himself in music. The group hadn’t performed together since 2016, but on Sunday (Nov. 15), Tangana, Sticky M.A., Jerv.AGZ, I-ACE and Fabianni reunited on stage at Madrid’s Movistar Arena. Related Westlife Sets 2027 North America Tour: Exclusive Lily Collins Pays Tribute to Phil Collins After Rock Hall Induction Watch Olivia Dean, Kehlani, Juanes & More Revealing 2027 Grammy Nominations Here Explore C.Tangana See latest videos, charts and news

The concert drew around 14,000 people, according to promoter Live in Dallas, and kicked off a four-night run at the venue that continues through Wednesday (Nov. 18).

Shortly after 9 p.m. local time, the screens lit up with old footage of the members when they were still teenagers. Then they appeared on stage in hoodies and pulled-up hoods, their faces barely visible in the near darkness. Sticky M.A. came out first to perform “To pue’ ser.” Tangana joined him for “Explícame,” kicking off a stripped-down set during which songs rolled one into the next with barely a pause — and hardly a word in between.

“What’s up, Madrid? Who knows this one?” they called out before “Balas perdidas.” The crowd answered, hands in the air and phones recording. After “Still Rapping,” one of the most loudly sung tracks of the opening stretch, the lights went out and a huge black curtain dropped. When it lifted, a set inspired by the cover of Siempre appeared, with oversized recreations of several objects from the artwork: a hamburger, a glass, a champagne bottle, a smoking ashtray and a giant skull. The DJ booth sat atop a gold bar engraved with “Oro Fino,” “AGZ” and “2016-2026.”

The collective’s roots go back to 2008, when Antón Álvarez — then known as Crema, and years later as Tangana — released a mixtape titled Agorazein . The name eventually became the group’s own. Emerging from Madrid’s underground rap scene, AGZ gradually folded melodies and trap elements into its sound, releasing the albums Kind of Red (2011) and Siempre (2016).

The show’s lighting and mood shifted as the set moved along. During Sticky M.A.’s “Diablo,” red beams shot from the skull’s eyes, creating one of the night’s most striking visuals. More than two hours, the concert balanced Agorazein songs with tracks from the members’ solo careers, including “Ya sabes,” “Mentira,” “Tentación,” “Spanish Jigga Freestyle” and “Yelo.”

entertainment.title: ‘Spirit of the Photobooth’ Doc Highlights the Invention’s Democratic Origins and Its Gen-Z Resurgence
entertainment.summary: The documentary played at the International Center of Photography as part of Art Week.
entertainment.body:
In honor of the 100th anniversary of the humble photobooth, a new documentary unveils its democratic origins, its place in history as means of self-expression and its recent resurgence among Gen-Z.

The documentary, entitled Spirit of the Photobooth , played an encore screening at the International Center of Photography Saturday as part of the inaugural Art Week from Artforum and ARTnews. The film, written and directed by Sam Anthony, first premiered in September.

As told in the film, Anatol Josepho, a Russian immigrant to the U.S., founded the automated analog photobooth as a means for everyday people to be able to get their own portraits, instead of the more expensive and time intensive process of sitting for a studio photo. The first photobooths were located just north of Times Square and caused a sensation in 1926, with crowds lining up for a chance in the booth until 4 a.m. The next year Josepho sold the patent for the booths for $1 million to businessman Henry Morgenthau, who launched booths across the nation.

From there, photo booths popped up at army bases, allowing soldiers to send home a photo, and expanded into Europe, where they were favored among members of the surrealist movement. The automated, private nature of the booths also gave Black Americans a chance for self-expression in the Jim Crow South, and gave queer couples an opportunity to take home private keepsakes, with some photobooths stationed in men’s bathrooms. Andy Warhol used photobooth strips as a basis for his pop art and silk screen painting, helping to legitimize it as a form of art.

While photobooths gradually fell into disuse, due to the rise of digital cameras and cell phones with cameras, a dedicated group of enthusiasts across the globe have worked to bring old booths back to life — the refurbishment is pricey, but the business of booths is quickly profitable — and to revive enthusiasm for the practice.

Happily, Gen-Z has since flocked to photobooths — with one owner noting it may be “some of the only analog tech” they’ve experienced — as enthusiasts say they’re in search of something tangible and real, and have seen the locations promoted on social media.The Old Friend Photobooth in lower Manhattan is one of the most popular current locations, with the Gen-Z owners now turning their attention to refurbishing a booth at Coney Island, the former mecca for photo booths from the 1940s through ‘70s.

entertainment.body:
Unless you’ve been living under a rock or have never set foot in any retail store, Ella Langley ‘s chart-topping country anthem “Choosin’ Texas” has been unavoidable over the last year.

The wildly catchy track, co-written by country icon Miranda Lambert, launched Langley into a new league, which was reflected in the 2027 Grammy Awards nominations . The 27-year-old was tied for the third-most nominated artist of the year, with seven nominations, four of which are in the general field categories.

Langley earned nods for best new artist, album of the year, song of the year and record of the year, along with best country song, best country solo performance and best contemporary country album. Through “Choosin’ Texas,” Langley’s represented in all general field categories, with collaborators Miranda Lambert and Joybeth Taylor getting nominated for producer of the year and songwriter of the year, non-classical. Released in October 2025, “Choosin’ Texas” has continued to dominate on the charts. The track, currently sitting at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, has spent 27 weeks atop the chart, making it the longest-running song to accomplish such a feat.

Langley is the only country artist nominated in the four major categories — album of the year, song of the year, record of the year and best new artist. Coming into the year, it was unclear whether or not the singer would even be eligible for the best new artist category. entertainment.title: The Longest-Leading Billboard Hot 100 No. 1s: ‘Choosin’ Texas’ & More
entertainment.summary: A select few hits have led the chart for at least 10 weeks — and 20-plus.
entertainment.body:
Beginning with Debby Boone’s “You Light Up My Life” in 1977, a relatively select few smashes have led the Billboard Hot 100 for at least 10 weeks. How few? Just a mere 4% of all Hot 100 No. 1s dating to the chart’s launch on Aug. 4, 1958, have earned the achievement.

Olivia Newton-John’s “Physical” flexed 10 weeks at No. 1 in 1981-82, and that smash and Boone’s shared the mark for the longest Hot 100 reign for more than a decade, until Boyz II Men’s “End of the Road” dominated for 13 weeks in 1992. That best lasted briefly, as Whitney Houston’s “I Will Always Love You” led for 14 weeks in late 1992/early 1993. In 1995-96, Mariah Carey and Boyz II Men’s “One Sweet Day” ran up 16 weeks at No. 1, a milestone that held for more than 23 years. (Songs began logging longer No. 1 stays after the Hot 100 adopted electronically tracked data, according to Luminate, in late 1991.)

In 2017, Luis Fonsi and Daddy Yankee’s “Despacito,” featuring Justin Bieber, tied the No. 1 run of “One Sweet Day.” By 2019, Lil Nas X’s “Old Town Road,” featuring Billy Ray Cyrus, collected 19 weeks atop the Hot 100, a mark matched by Shaboozey’s “A Bar Song (Tipsy)” beginning in July 2024.

On the Sept. 5, 2026-dated Hot 100, Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas” became the sole longest-leading non-holiday hit, with its 20th week at No. 1. As of the Nov. 21 survey, it’s the overall record holder with 28 weeks, having surpassed Mariah Carey’s “All I Want for Christmas Is You,” which has jingled to No. 1 for 22 weeks over each holiday season since December 2019.

In honor of the singles that have claimed the Hot 100’s top spot the longest, here’s a look at the elite leaders to rule for double-digit weeks.

“It feels surreal,” Langley told Billboard News earlier in 2026 of the song’s impact. “I think this has been the biggest moment for me, where I’ve seen where fans can change your career. For so long, you’re like, ‘Alright, one song at a time, one record at a time.’ But with this one song — and they’ve done it continuously for me — but really with ‘Choosin’ Texas’ … man, have they taken ahold of it. It’s wild.”
